# Primitive extrusion, its actual arithmetic roof, and zonotope coefficients

This note proves an exact measure identity for adding integer segments to
an actual convex body. It also gives an actual convex-body example showing
why the new coefficient measure cannot automatically be assigned the depth
of its lower-rank projection. The example is not a counterexample to OC.

Throughout, n>=1, d>=0. Mixed measure means the sum of d-dimensional
Lebesgue measures over integer base fibers; for d=0 it is counting measure.
No assertion about intrinsic q<d measure is made. All displayed identities
allow zero d-volume fibers and zero total mixed measure. A zero-dimensional
quotient base is a singleton with counting measure one.

## 1. Exact one-direction measure identity for every integer increment

Let C be a nonempty compact convex subset of R^n times R^d, let v be a
primitive integer vector, and put

    C_k=C+[0,k](v,0),                 k=0,1,2,... .

Write pi_v for the quotient of the integer coordinates by Rv, with quotient
lattice Z^n/Zv. Then

    mu_(n,d)(C_k)=mu_(n,d)(C)+k mu_(n-1,d)(pi_v C).              (1)

The quotient mixed measure is independent of the chosen integer basis of
the quotient lattice. This is an exact identity for every nonnegative
integer k, not an asymptotic or a large-width statement.

To prove it, use a unimodular change of integer coordinates sending v to
e_1; this preserves every continuous fiber measure and permutes the integer
bases bijectively. Write the coordinates as (t,w,x), with w in R^(n-1),
and let T=pi_v C. For each (w,x) in T, the actual line section of C is a
nonempty closed interval

    [a(w,x),b(w,x)].

It becomes [a(w,x),b(w,x)+k] in C_k. Its number of integer points is
floor(b)-ceil(a)+1, which is nonnegative even when the interval has no
integer point. Increasing b by integer k increases that number by exactly
k. Sum over integer w and integrate in x. Tonelli applies to nonnegative
indicators on a bounded set, giving (1). The same argument for d=0 is a
finite sum. Endpoints are counted exactly; no supporting interval is
replaced by an open one.

If v=c v_0 with v_0 primitive and c a positive integer, the same proof
gives an increment kc times the quotient mixed measure. The segment for
the negative vector has the same quotient coefficient, by using -v_0 as
the primitive coordinate. A zero vector has no effect.

## 2. The coefficient is an actual continuous mixed-volume coefficient

Keep the unimodular coordinates of Section 1. For each integer w put

    Q_w={(t,x):(t,w,x) in C},        T_w=projection_x(Q_w).

Fubini on the same real interval sections gives, for EVERY real s>=0,

    vol_(d+1)(Q_w+[0,s]e_1)=vol_(d+1)(Q_w)+s vol_d(T_w).        (2)

This includes lower-dimensional Q_w: an interval of initial length zero
still gains length s above every point of its projection. Empty sections
contribute zero. Summing (2) over integer w shows that the coefficient
in (1) is precisely the coefficient of s in this actual continuous
volume polynomial. In standard mixed-volume notation it is
(d+1)V(Q_w[d],[0,e_1]), summed over w. Formula (2) proves the coefficient
directly, so no mixed-volume theorem is needed for its value.

Lebesgue measure here is in the legitimate unimodular coordinates
(t,w,x). Equivalently, the freed integer line uses lattice-normalized
length. If Euclidean length along the original vector v is used instead,
the corresponding factor ||v|| must be restored. No arbitrary affine
normalization of the mixed lattice has been used.

## 3. Exact added-measure law and all ambient halfspaces

Let nu be quotient mixed measure on T, and define the finite Borel maps

    R_r(w,x)=(floor(b(w,x))+r,w,x),          r=1,...,k.

The upper endpoint b is upper semicontinuous on its compact convex domain,
hence Borel. These maps give the EXACT measure decomposition

    mu|_(C_k intersect Lambda)
       =mu|_(C intersect Lambda)+sum_(r=1)^k (R_r)_# nu.          (3)

Indeed the new integer points on every original real line section are
exactly floor(b)+1,...,floor(b)+k. They are distinct and lie outside the
original interval. Formula (3) remains valid when the original interval
had no integer sample. Each added law has total mass nu(T), although its
support need not be a mixed-integer intersection of a convex body.

In particular, for every CLOSED ambient halfspace

    H={alpha t+ell(w,x)>=beta},

one has

    mu(C_k intersect H)-mu(C intersect H)
      =sum_(r=1)^k integral_T
         1_{alpha(floor(b(w,x))+r)+ell(w,x)>=beta} dnu.           (4)

This is the exact oblique flux term. When alpha=0 it reduces to k times
the quotient mass in the corresponding halfspace. When alpha!=0 the
integer roof remains inside the integrand and cannot be discarded.
Every weak inequality in (4) retains its boundary mass.

## 4. A finite block formula, including genuine tail-depth credits

For this section suppose A=nu(T)>0. Let a_0 and b_0 be the global minimum
and maximum of t on C. Set h=ceil(b_0)-floor(a_0), and take integer
k>=h. There are N=k-h+1 full quotient copies at integer levels

    J={l,...,r},    l=ceil(b_0),    r=k+floor(a_0).

The other actual levels are exactly the following fixed projected tails:

    T^-_s=pi_v(C intersect {t<=s}),
       ceil(a_0)<=s<=ceil(b_0)-1,

    T^+_s=pi_v(C intersect {t>=s}),
       floor(a_0)+1<=s<=floor(b_0).

The left tails occur at t=s and the right tails at t=k+s. To verify this,
the level-t section of C_k is the projection of C restricted to
t-k<=t_original<=t. In the indicated left, full, and right ranges,
respectively, its lower bound, both bounds, and upper bound are redundant.
This proves the decomposition also when a_0 or b_0 is an integer.

Let D_U(y) denote the raw halfspace depth at any point y for the mixed
measure of a quotient set U; it is defined to be zero outside its convex
support. In a zero-dimensional quotient ambient space it is the whole
mass at the single point. Choose an actual y in T intersect the quotient
mixed lattice and put

    Q=D_T(y),   L=sum_s D_(T^-_s)(y),   R=sum_s D_(T^+_s)(y).

For every j in J, the SINGLE actual point (j,y) satisfies

    D_(C_k)(j,y)
       >= min{(j-l+1)Q+L, (r-j+1)Q+R}.                        (5)

For a through-point cap with alpha>=0, all full copies at levels >=j
and all right tails have nonnegative integer-coordinate margin. Their
restrictions therefore contain the quotient through-y halfspace, giving
the second bound. For alpha<=0 use the left copies and tails. If the
quotient normal vanishes, those favorable traces are entire quotient
sets, whose masses are at least their depths. A cap containing the point
can first be shifted through it, only decreasing mass. Thus (5) controls
all ambient directions and does not round a continuous center.

For Q>0, maximizing its right side over the finite set of actual levels
is exactly

    ((N+1)Q+L+R)/2 - Q dist(x_*,{0,...,N-1}),
    x_*=(N-1)/2+(R-L)/(2Q).                                   (6)

This follows by writing the minimum of the two affine expressions as
their mean minus Q times the distance to their crossing. In particular,
if |R-L|<=(N-1)Q, this is at least (NQ+L+R)/2. Formula (5), rather than
an unproved common-center assertion for the tails, is the valid budget.
The total mass in this block decomposition is NA+B, where B is the sum
of the tail masses; (1) also gives NA+B=mu(C)+kA.

For example, an exact half-depth induction at this y is sufficient if
Q=beta A, |R-L|<=(N-1)Q, and L+R>=beta B. The last inequality is NOT
automatic. Already C=conv{(0,-2),(0,-1),(1,1),(1,2)} has T=[-2,2],
whose unique deepest point is y=0. Its two tails at levels 0 and 1 are
[-2,-1] and [1,2], each of positive length but depth zero at y. This
counterexample concerns the proposed tail credit, not the depth of C_k.

## 5. A unit roof can have arbitrarily small maximum depth

Fix a positive integer N and consider the actual planar convex body

    C^(N)={(t,x):0<=x<=1, 0<=t<=N sqrt(x)}.

Convexity follows from concavity of sqrt(x); this is compact and has
nonempty interior. The integer direction e_1 is primitive. Its quotient
is the unit interval, of mass one and maximum raw depth 1/2. By (3),
the difference between the mixed measures of C^(N)+[0,1]e_1 and C^(N)
is the unit-mass law rho_N on

    t=j,   (j-1)^2/N^2<=x<j^2/N^2,       j=1,...,N,

together with the zero-length point (N+1,1). Every point of its positive
fibers has depth at most

    (4 sqrt(2N)+2)/N.                                          (7)

To prove this for an arbitrary (j_0,x_0) in that support, take the CLOSED
cap through it

    x-(2j_0/N^2)t <= x_0-2j_0^2/N^2.

If it captures a positive-length portion of the j-th roof fiber, then

    (j-1)^2 <= N^2 x_0+2j_0(j-j_0)
              <= j_0^2+2j_0(j-j_0),

so (j-j_0-1)^2<=2j_0<=2N. There are at most 2sqrt(2N)+1 such integer
indices. Each roof fiber has length (2j-1)/N^2<2/N. Multiplying proves
(7). At the extra point (N+1,1), the cap {t>=N+1} has zero rho_N mass.
The same upper bound therefore holds for every possible center in the
entire added roof set and its closure. No corresponding claim is made
about centers in the convex hull of that set.

For a concrete strict certificate take N=4096. Since 2N=8192<91^2,
the bound is strictly below 366/4096=183/2048<1/4. Thus even HALF of
the quotient's maximum depth cannot be guaranteed for this actual added
coefficient law. Letting N grow makes its maximum depth tend to zero.

The original and extruded bodies themselves are not counterexamples to
OC. The roof is their measure difference, not a convex induced mixed set.
The obstruction is specifically to assigning a universal quotient-depth
credit to an individual term of the exact coefficient decomposition (3).

For d>1 take the product with [0,1]^(d-1). The same cap, ignoring the
new continuous variables, proves (7) while the quotient is a unit cube
with maximum depth 1/2. Thus the obstruction persists in every continuous
dimension. Further products with binary integer cubes give the analogous
higher-integer-rank examples by finite tilts isolating each binary base.
More explicitly, with n-1 additional binary coordinates, the quotient
and added law both have total mass 2^(n-1). The quotient's maximum raw
depth is 1/2: central symmetry of its own cube gives the lower bound, and
a finite base tilt isolates the chosen cube for the matching upper bound.
The added law has maximum raw depth at most 183/2048 at N=4096, using
the tangent cap above and a finite binary-base isolating tilt. Thus its
normalized maximum is strictly less than half the quotient's normalized
maximum in every n>=1 and d>=1.

## 6. Exact arithmetic zonotope polynomial in any integer rank

Let v_1,...,v_m be any integer vectors, including dependent or nonprimitive
ones, and k_1,...,k_m nonnegative integers. For an independent subset I
define

    V_I=span_R{v_i:i in I},
    L_I=V_I intersect Z^n,
    m(I)=[L_I:sum_(i in I) Z v_i],
    A_I=mu_(n-|I|,d)(pi_I C),

where pi_I is quotient by V_I, with quotient lattice Z^n/L_I. Put
m(empty)=1 and A_empty=mu_(n,d)(C). Then

    mu_(n,d)(C+sum_i [0,k_i]v_i)
      =sum_(I independent) m(I) A_I product_(i in I) k_i.        (8)

All segments act only in the integer coordinates. The quotient lattice
is free because L_I is saturated, and choosing any integer basis of it
defines A_I unambiguously. These choices never transform the continuous
coordinates, so there is no fiber-volume Jacobian. Dependent subsets
have no term. In particular, for directions in a unimodular partial basis
all m(I)=1; successive-minimum vectors must not silently be assumed to
have this property.

Here is a proof by adding the segments one at a time. In any current
quotient lattice, a nonzero projected integer vector is c times a
primitive vector. Section 1 therefore adds k c times the mixed volume
of the further quotient; a projected zero vector adds nothing. Expand
recursively. A chain of projections contributes exactly when its original
vectors are independent. Its product of divisibilities is m(I).

To check the latter statement without an index shortcut, suppose I is
independent and v is independent of V_I. Let c be the divisibility of
the class of v in Z^n/L_I. Then

    [L_(I+v):L_I+Zv]=c,
    [L_I+Zv:(sum_(i in I)Zv_i)+Zv]=m(I).

The first equality follows because the saturation of the rank-one group
generated by that class has primitive generator v/c in the quotient.
The second follows because adjoining an independent vector changes none
of the relations within L_I. Multiplication of these two finite indices
gives m(I+v)=c m(I). This proves the coefficient in every expansion order
and completes the induction proving (8).

As an elementary arithmetic calibration, v_1=(1,0), v_2=(1,2), and
C={0} in R^2 with d=0 give

    #(C+[0,k_1]v_1+[0,k_2]v_2)=1+k_1+k_2+2k_1k_2.

Both vectors are primitive, but their pair has index two. At k_1=k_2=1
the four vertices and (1,1) are the five counted points. An index-one
formula would already fail here.
The same numerical calibration can be made full dimensional by replacing
C={0} by [-1/10,1/10]^2: its original and both one-dimensional quotient
lattice counts are still one, and (8) gives the same five points after
the two unit extrusions.

Equation (8) supplies actual, nonnegative arithmetic coefficient data
across affine-rank quotients. Equation (4) shows the additional roof
information required to use those data for oblique cap budgets. No OC
bound is inferred merely from coefficient positivity.

The supplementary verifier
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_primitive_extrusion_zonotope_roof_two_sided.py` passes 7,469 exact
checks, including nonlattice rational polygons, dependent/nonprimitive
directions, initially unsampled intervals, variable continuous simplex
fibers, the roof tangent inequality, and the finite tail-budget formula.
The proofs above do not depend on the computation.

## 7. A whole-body cap polynomial, retaining every actual projection

There is a universal use of the WHOLE flux which does not assign depth
to an isolated roof. Let

    Z_sym=sum_i [-k_i,k_i]v_i,

with the same integer vectors and integer lengths as Section 6. For EVERY
closed ambient halfspace H, one has

    mu((C+Z_sym) intersect H)
      >=sum_(I independent) m(I) product_(i in I)k_i
                    mu_(n-|I|,d)(pi_I(C intersect H)).           (9)

To prove it, write the integer part of the halfspace normal as a, and
choose epsilon_i in {-1,1} with epsilon_i a.v_i>=0. Translating any
point of C intersect H by sum_i s_i epsilon_i v_i, 0<=s_i<=k_i,
keeps it in H and puts it in C+Z_sym. Thus the left side contains

    (C intersect H)+sum_i [0,k_i]epsilon_i v_i.

Apply (8) to this actual compact convex cap. Changing the signs of
generators changes neither the projection spans nor the indices. This
proves (9), including empty or lower-dimensional caps and closed boundary
mass. If a.v_i=0, the full segment [-k_i,k_i]v_i may be used instead;
the corresponding factor k_i in (9) can then be replaced by 2k_i.

For one primitive direction, (9) reads

    mu((C+[-k,k]v) intersect H)
      >=mu(C intersect H)+k mu_(n-1,d)(pi_v(C intersect H)).      (10)

The coefficient one in this general inequality is sharp even for an
oblique cap. In coordinates (t,x), take C=[-2,2] times [-1/2,1/2]
and H={t+x>=0}. Every projected x has a proper original line cut;
exactly k new upper integer samples are captured and no new lower sample
is captured. The increment is exactly k times the projection length.

Equations (9)-(10) refer to the SAME actual H on every coefficient.
They cannot be replaced by separate choices of favorable projected caps
or unrelated centers. In particular, they are consistent with the roof
counterexample in Section 5. Their total-mass denominator is the exact
polynomial (8) evaluated at 2k_i, whereas their cap coefficients are the
actual projected-cap measures in (9). Positivity alone does not supply
the missing simultaneous lower bounds on those coefficients.
